decoration.title: 🌳 Decoration

sections.text: Levels of detail and file size

decoration.text: 🌳 Decoration A town of plain boxes is not a town. Decoration recipes add what makes it believable: doors and windows on the side that faces the street, flower boxes, lamps, trees in the gardens, towers at the gates, bridges that clear the river. They all follow the style rules, so you choose how much of each. Facades facade dresses the side of a volume that faces a street: door ( round : the share with a rounded top), windows (with shutters ), frames (stone around windows and doors); flower_boxes (with flowers , some glowing ), baskets beside the door, ivy climbing the wall (a foliage material that takes the season); emblem : a six-petal flower in relief above the door, a town's badge; lamp . With facade: {sides: {spacing: 4.5}} the other open walls (gables, backs, houses at the back of a plot) get plainer windows, further apart and without a door. Window glass is a single pane. Plants On ground features, decorate: [{recipe: plants, …}] sows shrubs, trees and flower beds, never on a volume. Models Small models (flowers, lamps, benches, trees…) live in libraries the style names ( models: [models.yaml] ) and are drawn as instances : one mesh, many copies, so a forest costs almost nothing. A model is made of parts ( box , cylinder , cone , blob , petals , ogive ) with colours and materials, or read from a binary glTF made elsewhere ( file: lamp.glb , in metres, y up). Place them on points: shape: {role: model, model: lamp, scale: [0.9, 1.1], turn: random} . Sow them on ground features: decorate: [{recipe: scatter, density: 0.01, models: {lily: 3, lamp: 1}, group: 8}] . Variety. A model can be built in several variants ( variants: 3 ): its parts move ( move , metres) and change size ( grow , a share) a little in each, and blobs bend out of round their own way ( wobble ; smooth: false for faceted, rings for how finely they are cut). Every copy picks a variant and changes its colour, warmth and size ( vary: {color: 0.12, warmth: 0.06, scale: [0.8, 1.3]} ). Cylinders can narrow to top_radius (trunks), and parts can be tipped over ( roll , degrees), so a cylinder can be a wheel. Gates as models. The ogive part is a pointed arch (width, straight sides, depth; with border , a frame), so a gate can be built as a model and placed on a point; gate_towers then skips the gates near points of that kind ( except_near: main_gate ). Keeping out of the way. Decorations keep off blocks ( clear ), lines with a width ( keep_off_lines ), models placed on their own and each other ( spacing ), and can keep to the edge of their feature ( edge ). Biomes A layer of categories ( -layer biome=biomes.json ) colours the terrain and sows vegetation: in the style, terrain.biomes gives each biome a colour and, optionally, decorate recipes that cover its cells, never on the map's polygons nor on its wide lines (rivers, roads). terrain: biomes: conifers: {color: "#5b6a49", decorate: [{recipe: scatter, density: 0.00015, models: {fir: 1}, scale: [3, 5]}]} meadow: {color: "#b7b47f"} Rivers and bridges Rivers always run below the ground around them. With a relief, every water feature with an axis and a width digs its channel: the water lies freeboard metres (0.6) under the lower bank and never rises downstream, the bed is depth metres (2) under it, and the ground meets the water at the river's edge. Bridges ( follow: level lines) that cross water keep their underside clearance metres (1.5) over it, reach out to dry ground and stand on abutments. In a live scene, where the terrain exists already, the water stays above_bed metres over the ground of its axis and bridges still clear it. Tall walls and gates Wall lines can carry battlements along their top ( battlements: {height, width, gap} ), and the gate_towers recipe can close each gate above an arch ( arch : metres from the ground), so a tall wall keeps its gate a gate. Levels of detail and file size Pieces carry simpler versions for when they look small on screen, and Go Renderer picks one: the terrain is written at full resolution and at every 2nd, 4th and 8th vertex, with skirts under the chunk edges; facade details and plants hide from far away; models can declare simpler versions ( levels: [{below: 0.06, parts: […]}, {below: 0.006}] , no parts = not drawn). To keep files light, quads share their four vertices, instanced models are written once for every chunk that uses them, corner stones are one column per corner, and boxes standing on the ground have no underside: the same town weighs about half.

overview.title: Welcome to Go Scene Builder 👋

sections.text: All the pages, in reading order

overview.text: Welcome to Go Scene Builder 👋 Go Scene Builder turns a flat map into a 3D scene you can walk through : you say what is where (a house here, a street there) and what things look like (stone walls, red roofs), and it builds the village. It reads three things: a map (the outlines of houses, streets, rivers), a relief (how high the ground is) and style rules (a text file saying what each kind of thing looks like). It writes a .glb scene that Go Renderer's viewer opens. Change the rules and the same map becomes another village. Is it for me? ✅ You have a map and want to see it in 3D . ✅ You want to design how a place looks by writing rules , not by modelling every house. ✅ You are not a programmer : maps and rules are text files, no code needed. Where to start Pick the line that sounds like you. If you… Read Time want to see an example right away The example island 5 min are new and want to build something 🏴‍☠️ The quest : a village from a map, in 6 levels 60 min want to know what goes in and out The pipeline 10 min want to write style rules : roofs, walls, materials Style rules — want facades, trees, lamps, rivers, gates Decoration — Try it without writing code Everything here is text files and two commands: one builds the scene, the other opens it. go run ./cmd/build-scene -map map.geojson -style style.yaml -out village.glb go run ../go-renderer/cmd/visor village.glb The quest gives you the files to start from. All the pages, in reading order The menu on the left (or the files in docs/ ) follows this order. Start Overview : this page The quest : six levels, from one house to a walled town The example island Guides The pipeline : the four stages Style rules Decoration 🚧 Not done yet Balconies and more decorations. Words you will meet Word What it means Terminal The window where you type commands: Terminal on macOS and Linux, PowerShell on Windows. Repository A project's folder of files, kept on GitHub. git clone <address> copies it to your computer. Scene Everything a 3D picture holds: ground, houses, trees, the sea, the sky and the sun. .glb file A 3D scene in one file, in the open glTF format: many programs (Blender among them) open and write it. Quest The tutorial of these docs: short levels, each ending with something that works and an achievement. The family Go Scene Builder is one of a family of small projects that work together: Project What it does Go Renderer draws 3D scenes and flat interfaces Go UI buttons, panels and whole applications Go UI for Android Android apps that look like Android's own Go Sound sound and music Go Scene Builder (this one) 3D scenes from a flat map Go Simulator simulations that change a scene Go Terrain Simulator ground shaped by rivers Go Climate Simulator weather and biomes Go Flora Simulator forests that grow Go Urban Simulator towns that grow Go Motion Simulator a scene that moves Go for 3DS Go on the Nintendo 3DS ⚠️ All of them are educational experiments , written with an AI assistant and pending review by their author: good for learning and playing, not for production.

style-rules.title: 🎨 Style rules
style-rules.text: 🎨 Style rules Style rules are where you decide what things look like. They are a YAML file read in cascade , like a style sheet: every rule whose selector matches a feature adds or replaces values, and the last one wins. So you write the general look first ("buildings are plastered, with tiled roofs") and then the exceptions ("shops with three floors or more have darker roofs"). A complete example units: m chunk: 0.5 # km: pieces are grouped in squares this big (larger for larger maps) environment: {sun: [235, 38]} # azimuth and elevation in degrees; water_level adds a sea; # vertical_scale exaggerates the relief seen from above models: [models.yaml] # libraries of small models (see decoration) terrain: {color: "#6b7f47", bands: [{above: 350, color: "#9e9e99", blend: 30}]} relations: facing: {when: {kind: street}, reach: 20} # which side of a block looks onto a street rows: {tolerance: 0.4} # walls closer than this are shared (not drawn) rules: - when: {kind: street} shape: {role: ground, width: "width * 1000", lift: 0.12} color: "#e6dcc4" - when: {kind: river} shape: {role: water, width: "width * 1000", above_bed: 1.8} - when: {kind: building} shape: {role: volume, height: "3.5 + (floors - 1) * 3"} walls: {color: "#e9dfc9"} roof: {recipe: gable, pitch: 38, ridge: long, eaves: 0.5, color: "#a4553a"} - when: {kind: building, use: [shop, workshop], floors: {min: 3}} roof: {color: "#8e4631"} - when: {kind: wall} shape: {role: line, height: 9, thickness: 3} openings: {where: {kind: street, class: road}, width: 6} # a gap where a road crosses it decorate: [{recipe: gate_towers, size: 6, height: 13}] # and a tower at each side of the gap - when: {kind: bridge} shape: {role: line, follow: level, thickness: "width * 1000", height: 0.4, sink: 0.8} - when: {kind: tower} shape: {role: point, size: 8, height: 15, form: round} The same map, two looks The example island has two style files for one map. Only the rules for houses and towers differ: style.yaml plasters the walls and tiles the roofs, style-stone.yaml builds them in masonry with slate hip roofs, stone frames, corner stones and ivy. style.yaml style-stone.yaml walls: {material: {pattern: plaster}} walls: {material: {pattern: masonry}} roof: {recipe: gable, pitch: 35, color: "#a4553a"} roof: {recipe: hip, pitch: 30, color: "#4a4f57"} stonework: {plinth: 0.6} stonework: {plinth: 0.8, quoins: {width: 0.45}} (A few lines of each, with one colour of each palette; the files have the rest.) Selectors and values A selector ( when ) uses Go Simulator's condition language: the kind , a property equal to a value or to one of a list, or a number within {min, max} . Values can be: numbers; #rrggbb colours, or "@name" : the colour in the feature's property name ; a palette , a list of colours: every feature takes one, always the same for the same id, so a street does not look painted from one bucket; arithmetic over the feature's numeric properties: "3.5 + (floors - 1) * 3" . Shapes: what a feature becomes Role Becomes ground a polygon (or a line widened by width ) draped lift metres over the relief: streets, gardens, squares water a level sheet above_bed metres over the bed under the feature's own line volume a block: walls from sink metres under the lowest ground under its corners up to height , where the roof starts line prisms of thickness and height in pieces of segment metres following the ground; with follow: level , one level prism whose top is height over its highest end, like a bridge deck point a square or round block of size metres, decorated like volumes model a model from a library, placed on a point (see decoration ) none nothing Materials Every part can set its material: material: {pattern: cobbles, scale: 0.35} : a procedural pattern ( cobbles , masonry , plaster , shingles , planks or grass , metres per cell) that Go Renderer draws on the fly: detail without textures or extra triangles; material: {kind: glow} : shines in the dark, like lanterns; material: {foliage: true} : takes the season's colour; material: {hide_below: 0.1} : hidden when it looks smaller than this share of the screen. Walls and roofs Volumes are dressed by recipes: walls : colour and material. Where a neighbour leans against a wall, only the part above its eaves is drawn. roof : recipe flat , gable or hip , with pitch (degrees), eaves (overhang, metres), color and ridge : long or short (the side of the footprint's rectangle the ridge follows), along_street or across_street (relative to the side that faces a street). Under a sloped roof the walls stand on the footprint's smallest rectangle, like the roof. roof.chimneys: {share, width, above} : stone chimneys on a share of the houses. stonework: {plinth, quoins} : a stone plinth and corner stones. Houses on slopes Houses stand halfway between their lowest and highest corners ( seat: middle , the default; or lowest , highest ): on a slope they are cut into the hill uphill and rise on a stone base downhill. A door above the street gets stone steps down to it, and the plinth leaves the door and its steps free. A footprint that is not nearly a rectangle keeps its walls on the footprint, so they meet the neighbours' exactly, under a roof sloping from every side. Terrain terrain sets the ground's color , its material, and bands : colours above a height ( {above, color, blend} ), for rock or snow. With a layer of biomes, terrain.biomes colours each biome and sows its plants ( decoration ).

the-example-island.title: 🏝️ The example island
the-example-island.text: 🏝️ The example island A small made-up island to try the builder with: about 1.6 by 1.2 kilometres of sea and land, a hill of about 150 metres in the north-east with a forest on it, a river running down to the west coast, a beach along the south-west bay and a village of about a hundred houses on two crossing streets around a square. Everything in it is invented, and its numbers are round. The files All in examples/island/ : File What it is map.geojson The map, in metres east and north of the island's centre, one feature per line. Kinds: building (with floors and use ), street , road and path (lines with a width in metres), square , garden , forest and beach (polygons), river and bridge (lines with a width ), tower and lamp (points). relief.json , relief.f32 The relief: 160 × 120 cells of 10 metres. Under 0 metres is the sea floor. style.yaml The full style: plastered houses with tiled gable roofs, facades, gardens with plants, a forest of models, a river and a bridge, a sea at 0 metres. style-stone.yaml The same, with stone houses and slate hip roofs ( style rules ). style-plain.yaml Shapes only, without decoration ( decoration ). models.yaml The model library: a fir, a broadleaf tree and a lamp. Build it From the repository's root (GEOS must be installed): go run ./cmd/build-scene -map examples/island/map.geojson -relief examples/island/relief.json \ -style examples/island/style.yaml -out island.glb It prints how long each stage took, about 33 pieces and 130,000 triangles, and no warnings. Swap style.yaml for style-stone.yaml or style-plain.yaml to build the other looks from the same map. Look at it Open the scene with Go Renderer's viewer, from the go-renderer folder: go run ./cmd/visor path/to/island.glb How the pictures were made Every picture of a scene in these docs is one frame of Go Renderer's viewer, captured with -capture in a 1440 × 900 window ( -width 1440 -height 900 ) and then reduced. Scene coordinates are kilometres, x east and z south, so the village's main street is near x = -0.40, z = 0.218 ( visor is go run ./cmd/visor in Go Renderer): visor -capture island.png island.glb # the whole island visor -capture village.png -look-at=-0.17,0.16 -zoom 0.14 island.glb # the village from above visor -capture square.png -look-at=-0.20,0.205 -zoom 0.07 island.glb # the square, close visor -capture forest.png -look-at=0.2,-0.15 -zoom 0.12 island.glb # the forest on the hill visor -capture street.png -walk -eye-height 0.0017 -look-at=-0.40,0.218 \ -heading 85 -pitch 0 island.glb # down the main street visor -capture street-night.png -night -walk -eye-height 0.0017 \ -look-at=-0.40,0.218 -heading 85 -pitch 0 island.glb # the same, at night The flat map and the shaded relief were drawn from the same files with a short script; they are drawings, not output of the builder.

the-pipeline.title: 🗺️ The pipeline
the-pipeline.text: 🗺️ The pipeline A map says where things are: this polygon is a house, this line is a street. It does not say what a house looks like. Go Scene Builder adds that, following style rules written by you, so the same map can become a stone town or a timber village just by changing the rules. It knows nothing about any particular world: the map and the rules do. Basic blocks. The relief becomes terrain; ground features (streets, gardens, squares) are draped over it; water lies level; houses become volumes; walls and bridges become lines that follow the ground; points become small blocks or models. Relations. What a block cannot know alone: which side of a house looks onto a street, which walls neighbours share (so they are not drawn twice), where a road crosses a wall and opens a gate. Style rules. A cascade, like a style sheet: general rules first, specific ones after, the last that matches wins. Decoration. Recipes add roofs, facades with doors and windows, towers at gates, plants in gardens and models such as lamps and benches. Run it GEOS must be installed ( pkg-config geos ). go run ./cmd/build-scene -map map.geojson -relief relieve.json -style style.yaml -out scene.glb go run ./cmd/build-scene -map map.geojson -relief relieve.json -layer biome=biomes.json -style style.yaml -out scene.glb It prints how long each stage took and the first warnings (features no rule styles, wrong values). -profile cpu.out writes a CPU profile for go tool pprof . Then open the scene: go run ./cmd/visor scene.glb in Go Renderer. The example island is a complete set of inputs to try it with. What goes in The map is a GeoJSON FeatureCollection . Every feature has properties.id (stable between versions) and properties.kind (a free word: the rules give it a meaning); any other property can be read by the rules ( floors , use , width …). The collection's properties say how to read the coordinates: units ( km or m ), axes ( east-north or east-south ) and origin (the point the scene is centred on). {"type": "FeatureCollection", "properties": {"units": "m", "axes": "east-north", "origin": [0, 0]}, "features": [ {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"id": "main-street", "kind": "street", "width": 8}, "geometry": {"type": "LineString", "coordinates": [[-430, -220], [-260, -210], [-200, -210]]}} ]} The relief is relieve.json , {"columns", "rows", "cell", "west", "north", "units"} with the edges of the grid, and next to it relieve.f32 : heights in metres as little-endian float32, row by row from the north, each at the centre of its cell. Without a relief the ground is flat. The header can have any name: the values are read from the same path with .f32 instead of .json (the example island's are relief.json and relief.f32 ). Layers are grids of categories in the same format with labels (the name of every value), such as the biomes a climate simulator writes: -layer biome=biomes.json . They colour the terrain and sow vegetation ( decoration ). What comes out A binary glTF 2.0 file, quantised to take less room. Scene coordinates are in kilometres, x east, y up, z south, centred on the origin. Pieces are grouped by material in squares of chunk km (0.5 by default) so the viewer only draws those in sight; terrain pieces are marked walkable ( ground ). The scene's extras carry the sun, fog, an optional sea and the vertical scale, which Go Renderer reads . As a library Go Simulator uses the builder to draw growing towns live with the same style rules. build.Build takes the same inputs as the command plus Heights (any source of ground heights, for a scene whose terrain exists already), Detail (the longest side of draped triangles without a relief) and Context (features that take part in the relations without being built, such as the streets around a house being rebuilt). Status Done: reading maps, reliefs and rules; the basic blocks; the relations between blocks; recipes for walls, roofs (flat, gable, hip), gate towers, facades (door, windows, shutters, flower boxes, an emblem, lamps) and plants; materials with procedural patterns and glowing materials; colour palettes; models drawn as instances; biomes; levels of detail; rivers and bridges; the .glb writer; build-scene ; and use as a library from Go Simulator. Next: balconies and more decorations.

the-quest.title: The Go Scene Builder quest
the-quest.text: The Go Scene Builder quest Turn a flat map into a village you can walk through, one level at a time. Each level teaches one piece of Go Scene Builder and ends with a new scene in Go Renderer's viewer. The quest map: a road from START through 6 levels — Surveyor, Mason, Street builder, Geographer, Waterman and Gardener — to a final challenge, Town founder We will build a village : houses along a street, a square with a fountain, a garden, a river with a bridge, lamps that light up at night, and in the end a wall round it all, with gates. Every level has the same shape: the idea (explained with something from everyday life), the files , a checkpoint to know it works, and an optional bonus . You write two files and keep growing them: map.geojson (what is where) and style.yaml (what things look like). Before you start You need Go 1.25, GEOS ( sudo apt install libgeos-dev , brew install geos ) and Go Renderer's viewer to look at the result: git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-scene-builder git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-renderer mkdir village && cd village Keep two commands at hand; after each change, build and look: # build the scene go run ../go-scene-builder/cmd/build-scene -map map.geojson -style style.yaml -out village.glb # look at it: drag to turn, scroll to zoom, Tab to walk, N for the night go run ../go-renderer/cmd/visor village.glb The pictures were taken with -look-at 0,0 -zoom 0.45 added to the viewer. This is where everything will live by the end: village/ ├── map.geojson ← every level ├── style.yaml ← every level ├── relief/main.go ← level 4: writes the two files below ├── relieve.json ├── relieve.f32 └── models.yaml ← level 6 Level 1 · The Surveyor Mission Pieces Time One house on a meadow GeoJSON features, ground and volume shapes, a gable roof 8 min The idea A surveyor draws a plan: this outline is a house, that one a field. The plan says where , never how it looks . That is the style's job, like a dress code for a party: "houses wear cream walls and a red roof". Change the dress code and the same plan becomes another village. Every feature on the map has an id (its name, stable from one version to the next) and a kind (a free word: house , meadow ; the style gives it a meaning). Build it map.geojson , in metres, x to the east and y to the north, centred ten metres south of zero: { "type": "FeatureCollection", "properties": {"units": "m", "axes": "east-north", "origin": [0, -10]}, "features": [ {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"id": "meadow", "kind": "meadow"}, "geometry": {"type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [[[-60, 30], [60, 30], [60, -60], [-60, -60], [-60, 30]]]}}, {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"id": "house-1", "kind": "house", "floors": 2}, "geometry": {"type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [[[-4, 4], [4, 4], [4, 14], [-4, 14], [-4, 4]]]}} ] } style.yaml : units: m environment: {sun: [220, 35]} rules: - when: {kind: meadow} shape: {role: ground} color: "#8fa35a" - when: {kind: house} shape: {role: volume, height: 6} walls: {color: "#e9dfc9"} roof: {recipe: gable, pitch: 38, color: "#a4553a"} ground drapes a polygon over the ground; volume raises a block from it, height metres up to where the roof starts. Checkpoint The build prints [ground 1 volume 1] , and the viewer shows a cream house with a red roof on a green meadow. Level 1: one house with a red gable roof on a green meadow Bonus (optional): a flat roof Make the house a modern box with a flat roof and grey walls. Achievement unlocked: Surveyor Learn more: The pipeline · Style rules Level 2 · The Mason Mission Pieces Time Five houses, each its own height and colour properties, arithmetic, palettes, the cascade 8 min The idea Rules work like a style sheet , in cascade : every rule that matches adds its values, and when two say the same thing, the later one wins. Write the general look first ("houses have gable roofs") and the exceptions after ("shops have hip roofs"). A palette is a box of paint pots: each house takes one, always the same one for the same id, so the street does not look painted from one bucket. Build it Add four houses to the map's features (the map can say anything the style reads: here floors and use ): {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"id": "house-2", "kind": "house", "floors": 1}, "geometry": {"type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [[[6, 4], [14, 4], [14, 12], [6, 12], [6, 4]]]}}, {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"id": "house-3", "kind": "house", "floors": 3}, "geometry": {"type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [[[16, 4], [24, 4], [24, 15], [16, 15], [16, 4]]]}}, {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"id": "house-4", "kind": "house", "floors": 2}, "geometry": {"type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [[[-14, 4], [-6, 4], [-6, 13], [-14, 13], [-14, 4]]]}}, {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"id": "house-5", "kind": "house", "floors": 2, "use": "shop"}, "geometry": {"type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [[[-4, -4], [6, -4], [6, -13], [-4, -13], [-4, -4]]]}} Replace the house rule, and add the shop's exception after it: - when: {kind: house} shape: {role: volume, height: "3 + (floors - 1) * 3"} walls: {color: ["#e9dfc9", "#efe4cf", "#e2d2b4", "#f1ead9"]} roof: {recipe: gable, pitch: 38, ridge: long, eaves: 0.4, color: ["#a4553a", "#9a4b33", "#b0613f"], chimneys: {share: 0.5}} stonework: {plinth: 0.6, quoins: true} - when: {kind: house, use: shop} roof: {recipe: hip, color: "#6f6a64"} "3 + (floors - 1) * 3" reads each house's floors : three metres for the ground floor and three for each one above. chimneys: {share: 0.5} puts one on half of the houses; stonework adds a stone base and corner stones. Checkpoint Five houses of one, two and three floors, in slightly different creams and reds, two with chimneys; the shop's roof is grey and slopes on four sides. Level 2: five houses, one with a grey hip roof Bonus (optional): tall shops Shops with three floors or more get darker walls. Selectors take a number range. Achievement unlocked: Mason Level 3 · The Street builder Mission Pieces Time A street, a square, and doors facing the street lines with a width, materials, relations, facades 10 min The idea A house alone does not know where its front door goes. It needs to look around : which of its sides faces a street? That is a relation , worked out between blocks after they are built, like neighbours who know which house is opposite. The facade recipe then dresses that side with a door, windows with shutters and flower boxes. Build it Add a street (a line, widened by its width ) and a square: {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"id": "high-street", "kind": "street", "width": 6}, "geometry": {"type": "LineString", "coordinates": [[-60, 0], [60, 0]]}}, {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"id": "square", "kind": "square"}, "geometry": {"type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [[[10, -4], [26, -4], [26, -16], [10, -16], [10, -4]]]}} The whole style now: units: m environment: {sun: [220, 35]} relations: facing: {when: {kind: street}, reach: 20} rules: - when: {kind: meadow} shape: {role: ground} color: "#8fa35a" - when: {kind: street} shape: {role: ground, width: "width", lift: 0.3} color: "#d8cdb4" - when: {kind: square} shape: {role: ground, lift: 0.3} color: "#c9bfa8" material: {pattern: cobbles, scale: 0.4} - when: {kind: house} shape: {role: volume, height: "3 + (floors - 1) * 3"} walls: {color: ["#e9dfc9", "#efe4cf", "#e2d2b4", "#f1ead9"]} roof: {recipe: gable, pitch: 38, ridge: along_street, eaves: 0.4, color: ["#a4553a", "#9a4b33", "#b0613f"], chimneys: {share: 0.5}} stonework: {plinth: 0.6, quoins: true} facade: door: {color: "#5b3a26", round: 0.5} windows: {shutters: ["#2f5d50", "#7a3b2e"]} flower_boxes: {share: 0.5, flowers: ["#d23c4f", "#f2c14e"]} sides: {spacing: 4.5} - when: {kind: house, use: shop} roof: {recipe: hip, color: "#6f6a64"} relations.facing : sides within 20 metres of a street face it. lift: 0.3 keeps the street a little over the meadow, so the two do not flicker. material: {pattern: cobbles} draws paving stones on the square with no texture: Go Renderer makes the pattern as it draws. ridge: along_street : the roof's ridge runs along the street. facade.sides gives the other walls plainer windows, further apart. Checkpoint The build says 5 facing a street . Each house has a door and windows on its street side, some with flowers; the square is paved. Level 3: houses facing a street, with doors and windows, and a paved square Bonus (optional): ivy and lamps by the doors Achievement unlocked: Street builder Learn more: Decoration: facades Level 4 · The Geographer Mission Pieces Time Ground with a slope, and houses that stand on it the relief, terrain colours 10 min The idea A relief is a chessboard of heights : every square says how high the ground is there. It lives in two files: a small label ( relieve.json : how many squares, how big, where) and the heights themselves ( relieve.f32 : one number per square, row by row from the north). Houses on a slope stand halfway between their lowest and highest corners: cut into the hill uphill, on a stone base downhill. Build it Write the relief with a small Go program, relief/main.go : // Command relief writes the ground the village stands on: relieve.json, the grid's size and // place, and relieve.f32, a height in metres for every cell, row by row from the north. package main import ( "encoding/binary" "encoding/json" "log" "math" "os" ) func main() { const ( columns, rows = 80, 70 // cells cell = 2.0 // metres a side west, north = -80.0, 70.0 ) heights := make([]float32, 0, columns*rows) for row := range rows { for column := range columns { east := west + (float64(column)+0.5)*cell northing := north - (float64(row)+0.5)*cell heights = append(heights, float32(height(east, northing))) } } header := map[string]any{"columns": columns, "rows": rows, "cell": cell, "west": west, "north": north, "units": "m"} content, _ := json.Marshal(header) if err := os.WriteFile("relieve.json", content, 0o644); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } file, err := os.Create("relieve.f32") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } defer file.Close() if err := binary.Write(file, binary.LittleEndian, heights); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } // height is a slope rising to the north, a little rolling, down to a valley in the south. func height(east, north float64) float64 { slope := 0.12 * north rolling := 1.5 * math.Sin(east/14) * math.Cos(north/18) valley := -4 * math.Exp(-math.Pow((north+38)/14, 2)) return 20 + slope + rolling + valley } go mod init example.com/village # once, for the program go run ./relief # writes relieve.json and relieve.f32 The terrain now replaces the meadow: remove the meadow from the map and its rule from the style, and add to the style, under environment : terrain: {color: "#8fa35a", bands: [{above: 26, color: "#7d8f4c", blend: 3}]} Build with the relief: go run ../go-scene-builder/cmd/build-scene -map map.geojson -relief relieve.json -style style.yaml -out village.glb Checkpoint The ground rises to the north and rolls a little; the street follows it, the houses stand on it with stone bases where it falls away, and the ground is darker above 26 metres. Level 4: the village on a gentle slope Bonus (optional): snowy tops Achievement unlocked: Geographer Learn more: Houses on slopes · The pipeline: what goes in Level 5 · The Waterman Mission Pieces Time A river in the valley, and a bridge over it water shapes, level lines 8 min The idea Water always lies level , and a river digs its own bed : with a relief, the builder cuts a channel so the water stays under its banks and never runs uphill. A bridge is a plank laid level from one bank to the other, high enough for the water to pass under. Build it Add the river, the bridge and a lane from the street to it: {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"id": "river", "kind": "river", "width": 10}, "geometry": {"type": "LineString", "coordinates": [[-60, -40], [0, -32], [60, -44]]}}, {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"id": "bridge", "kind": "bridge", "width": 4}, "geometry": {"type": "LineString", "coordinates": [[8, -20], [8, -52]]}}, {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"id": "lane", "kind": "street", "width": 4}, "geometry": {"type": "LineString", "coordinates": [[8, -4], [8, -20]]}} And two rules, before the houses: - when: {kind: river} shape: {role: water, width: "width"} - when: {kind: bridge} shape: {role: line, follow: level, thickness: "width", height: 0.5} color: "#9c9486" material: {pattern: masonry, scale: 0.5} Checkpoint A blue river crosses the valley in the south, in a channel of its own; a stone bridge carries the lane over it. Level 5: a river in the valley and a stone bridge over it Bonus (optional): the sea Achievement unlocked: Waterman Learn more: Rivers and bridges Level 6 · The Gardener Mission Pieces Time A garden, lamps that light at night, a fountain and benches plants, model libraries, glow 10 min The idea A model library is a box of toys : a lamp, a fountain, a bench, each built once from simple parts (boxes, cylinders, cones, blobs). The map places them, or a recipe sows them over a ground, and Go Renderer draws every copy of a toy in one go, so a hundred cost no more than one. Build it models.yaml , in metres, the origin on the ground: models: lamp: parts: - {shape: cylinder, radius: 0.06, height: 3, color: "#2b2b2b"} - {shape: box, size: [0.3, 0.4, 0.3], at: [0, 3, 0], color: "#ffd98a", material: {kind: glow}} fountain: parts: - {shape: cylinder, radius: 1.6, height: 0.5, sides: 16, color: "#b9b2a5"} - {shape: cylinder, radius: 1.3, height: 0.52, sides: 16, color: "#5d8fb0"} - {shape: cylinder, radius: 0.2, height: 1.4, color: "#b9b2a5"} bench: parts: - {shape: box, size: [1.6, 0.08, 0.4], at: [0, 0.42, 0], color: "#6b4a2e"} - {shape: box, size: [0.1, 0.42, 0.4], at: [-0.7, 0, 0], color: "#3b3b3b"} - {shape: box, size: [0.1, 0.42, 0.4], at: [0.7, 0, 0], color: "#3b3b3b"} The lamp's glass is glow : it shines in the dark. Add a garden, two lamps and the fountain: {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"id": "garden", "kind": "garden"}, "geometry": {"type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [[[-24, -4], [-6, -4], [-6, -18], [-24, -18], [-24, -4]]]}}, {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"id": "lamp-1", "kind": "lamp"}, "geometry": {"type": "Point", "coordinates": [-2, 3]}}, {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"id": "lamp-2", "kind": "lamp"}, "geometry": {"type": "Point", "coordinates": [15, 3]}}, {"type": "Feature", "properties": {"id": "fountain", "kind": "fountain"}, "geometry": {"type": "Point", "coordinates": [18, -10]}} In the style, name the library after units : models: [models.yaml] and add, before the houses: - when: {kind: garden} shape: {role: ground, lift: 0.05} color: "#6f8f44" material: {pattern: grass, scale: 0.5} decorate: [{recipe: plants, density: 0.2, trees: 0.3, beds: 0.3, clear: 1}] - when: {kind: lamp} shape: {role: model, model: lamp} - when: {kind: fountain} shape: {role: model, model: fountain} - when: {kind: square} decorate: [{recipe: scatter, density: 0.01, models: {bench: 1}, edge: true}] The square's second rule adds to the first: the cascade again. Checkpoint Shrubs, trees and flower beds in the garden, a fountain in the square, benches at its edge, lamps by the street. Press N in the viewer: the lamps glow. Level 6: a garden of shrubs and trees beside the houses, a fountain in the square Level 6 at night: the lamps glow by the street Bonus (optional): a flowerbed of lilies Sow lilies over the garden, with a model of your own.
